claims.text: The origin of COVID-19 remains disputed between two main hypotheses.
Proponents of zoonosis argue that the earliest known cases cluster tightly around the Huanan Seafood Market.
Zoonosis proponents take the market clustering as strong evidence that the virus spilled over from animals sold there.
Critics argue that the market clustering may reflect where testing and surveillance were concentrated rather than where the outbreak began.
The market pattern is not decisive according to critics of the zoonosis hypothesis.
The Wuhan Institute of Virology conducted research on bat coronaviruses nearby.
Lab-leak supporters argue that WIV research raises the prior probability of an accidental escape.
Proximity alone establishes opportunity, not occurrence, according to lab-leak critics.
No direct evidence of an infected lab worker has been produced.
The furin cleavage site in the virus is unusual.
Some treat the furin cleavage site as a signature of engineering.
Similar features occur in natural coronaviruses, so the furin cleavage site does not by itself favor a laboratory origin.

links.rationale: [1] supplies the empirical premise that [2] interprets as decisive evidence for zoonosis
links.assumption: observed spatial clustering around the market is best explained by a local animal spillover rather than by surveillance patterns

links.rationale: [3] offers an alternative causal explanation that undercuts the inference drawn in [2]
links.assumption: differential testing intensity can produce apparent clustering without reflecting the true geographic origin

links.rationale: [3] directly entails the non-decisiveness conclusion stated in [4]
links.assumption: if clustering may be an artifact of surveillance, the pattern cannot be treated as decisive proof of origin

links.rationale: [5] supplies the factual premise that [6] uses to raise the prior for lab leak
links.assumption: conducting relevant coronavirus research at a nearby facility increases the baseline probability of a laboratory incident

links.rationale: [7] distinguishes possibility from actuality, weakening the inferential step in [6]
links.assumption: mere geographic proximity establishes opportunity but supplies no evidence that an actual escape occurred

links.rationale: [8] provides a concrete instance of the opportunity-versus-occurrence gap asserted in [7]
links.assumption: absence of direct evidence of an infected worker illustrates that opportunity has not been shown to have been realized

links.rationale: [9] supplies the premise that [10] interprets as an engineering signature
links.assumption: an unusual molecular feature is more likely to be the product of deliberate engineering than of natural evolution

links.rationale: [11] undercuts the uniqueness premise required by the engineering inference in [10]
links.assumption: natural occurrence of similar sites in wild coronaviruses removes the need to invoke laboratory manipulation
